food.text: Chilli pepper, now one of the most important spices in Indian cooking, arrived only in the 16th century. The Portuguese introduced it from Mexico, and it took its place beside older flavourings such as black mustard seed, cardamom, cumin and turmeric.

The famine of 1629 to 1632 in the Deccan and Gujarat was one of the worst in India's history. In the first 10 months of 1631 an estimated 3 million people perished in Gujarat and one million in the Deccan. It eventually killed the rich as well as the poor.

The British East India Company arrived in India in 1600, and by 1760 men were returning home with money and a taste for Indian food. In 1784 a listing in the Morning Herald and Daily Advertiser promoted ready-mix curry powder for Indian-style dishes.

One theory holds that the Portuguese introduced the technique of "breaking" milk with acid to Bengal in the 17th century. If so, Indian acid-set cheeses such as paneer and chhena were first made there. The Portuguese also brought a smoked cheese called Bandel, which is distinct from paneer.

The Qutb Shahi dynasty, centred in the city of Hyderabad, promoted the native cuisine along with their own. Modern Hyderabadi cuisine evolved under the Nizams from the mid-17th century and became a princely legacy, with most of its modern desserts introduced or invented in their time.

Southern India produced several notable cookbooks in this era: Soopa Shastra in 1508, Bhojana Kutuhala in 1675 and Sivatattva Ratnakara in 1699. They include both vegetarian and non-vegetarian cooking, except Soopa Shastra, which is a Jain vegetarian cookbook.

Kedgeree, recorded by 1790, derived from the simple Indian rice and lentil dish khichari. The Anglo-Indian version added garnishes of hard-boiled egg, fish and fried onions. The British version used smoked haddock and dropped the lentils.

In Vikrami Samwat 1720, or 1663 CE, the rains failed across all of Rajasthan. Many people died in Marwar and grain prices rose very high. A Jain traveller noted that grain was simply not to be had, and cattle perished in great numbers.
In 1664 the rains were normal in Rajasthan, yet a local famine struck Sojhat. Large numbers of people migrated, and many were sold away.

art.text: Under Jahangir, who took the throne after Akbar and ruled 1605 to 1627, Mughal painters worked on single pieces rather than collaborating as they had under Akbar. This period saw the emergence of distinct individual styles. Jahangir himself could identify the work of each artist, even when it was unnamed.

Shah Jahan, who ruled from 1628 to 1658, is best known architecturally for the Taj Mahal. Paintings under his rule were more formal than those of his predecessor, featuring court scenes rather than personal styles.

Mughal builders fused Islamic-Persian design with Hindustani art, and mosques and tombs were their most common large buildings. These were often topped by large domes and made extensive use of arches, features hardly used in Hindu temple architecture. They also avoided the figurative sculpture that was so important to Hindu temples.

Aurangzeb, who forcibly took the throne from his father Shah Jahan, held increasingly orthodox Sunni beliefs. In 1680 he banned music and painting. His reign saw the decline of Mughal patronage of the arts.

Lahore, an occasional residence of Mughal rulers, holds many important imperial buildings. Among them are the Badshahi Mosque, built 1673 to 1674, the fortress of Lahore with its famous Alamgiri Gate, and the colourful Wazir Khan Mosque, built 1634 to 1635.

Later Mughal architecture under Aurangzeb, who ruled 1658 to 1707, includes the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore and Bibi ka Maqbara in Aurangabad. By the late 18th century the Mughal style was effectively over.

In the later half of the 18th century, East India Company merchants provided a large market for native art. A genre of watercolour painting on paper and mica developed, showing everyday life, princely court regalia, and festivals and rituals. Called the company style or Patna style, it flourished first in Murshidabad.

By the sixteenth century, Dravidian temple architecture had reached its final form in Southern India. Its towers over the sanctuary, called vimana, are shorter and more pyramidal than the taller shikharas of the north.

Jahangir's reign gave rise to distinct individual painters, notably Bishan Das, Manohar Das, Abu al-Hasan, Govardhan, and Daulat. Two works created under his rule were the Razmnama, a Persian translation of the Hindu epic Mahabharata, and Jahangir's illustrated memoir, the Tuzuk-i Jahangiri.

The Shahjahan Mosque at Thatta in Sindh was built under Shah Jahan, and probably largely by him, yet it strongly reflects Central Asian Islamic style. The emperor had recently been campaigning near Samarkand.

After the Mughal style faded, versions called post-Mughal were widely adopted by the rulers of princely states and other wealthy people of all religions for palaces and tombs. Hindu patrons often mixed Hindu temple and palace architecture with Mughal elements and, later, European ones.

The innumerable Chaukhandi tombs of Sindh were constructed between the 16th and 18th centuries, but they do not resemble Mughal architecture. Their stonemason works show typical Sindhi workmanship, probably from before Islamic times.

war.text: On 16 March 1527 at Khanwa, in modern Rajasthan, Babur's Mughal Empire fought Rana Sanga's Kingdom of Mewar for supremacy of Northern India. It was one of the first battles in Northern India where gunpowder was used: Mughal muskets shot the charging Rajput army down in great numbers, and the noise of the muskets frightened the Rajputs' horses and elephants, which trampled their own men. The Mughals won, but both Timurids and Rajputs suffered heavy casualties, and dead bodies of both sides could be found as far as Bayana, Alwar and Mewat. Afterwards Babur ordered a tower of enemy skulls to be erected.

The First Luso-Malabarese War, which erupted in 1500 over trade, was the first armed conflict fought by the Portuguese Empire in Asia. It was the first of nine against the Zamorin of Calicut. It began after an armed mob attacked the Portuguese trading post at Calicut and killed about 50 Portuguese, and Cabral answered by killing the crews of ten seized ships and bombarding the city, which killed an estimated 500 to 600 people. Hostilities lasted thirteen years, until the Zamorin was assassinated (Albuquerque persuaded the pro-Portuguese heir to have him poisoned) and his successor signed a peace treaty with Afonso de Albuquerque.

In 1739 Nader Shah, emperor of Iran, defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal. He then captured and sacked Delhi, carrying away treasures including the Peacock Throne. Ahmad Shah Durrani later sacked Delhi in 1757, and by then the Mughal dynasty was reduced to puppet rulers.

Babur raided Punjab in 1504 and 1518, then in 1520-21 easily captured Bhira and Sialkot, known as the twin gateways to Hindustan. He later annihilated the Lodi sultanate's army at the First Battle of Panipat, where he killed the Sultan and founded the Mughal Empire.

In January 1508 Dom Lourenço de Almeida was escorting allied trade ships to Chaul when a joint Mamluk and Gujarati fleet attacked his squadron at anchor. He was killed when his flagship was sunk while he commanded a withdrawal. The battle of Chaul proved a pyrrhic victory for the Muslims. His father, the viceroy Dom Francisco de Almeida, then determined to destroy the Mamluk fleet and avenge his son, and routed it at Diu.

In 1737 the Maratha general Bajirao invaded and plundered Delhi. The Mughal Emperor sent 8,000 troops under Amir Khan Umrao Al Udat to drive off 5,000 Maratha cavalry, but Baji Rao easily routed the novice Mughal general.

The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686 to 1690 was fought between the Mughal Empire and the British East India Company in the late 17th century. The name 'Anglo-Mughal War' has also been used for other later conflicts, including the Carnatic Wars of 1744 to 1763.

The commercial colonization of India is dated to 1757, after the Battle of Plassey, when the Nawab of Bengal surrendered his dominions to the British East India Company. In 1765 the Company was granted the diwani, the right to collect revenue in Bengal and Bihar.
In 1523 Alam Khan Lodi invited Babur to invade but demanded Delhi once it was conquered. Babur refused, so Alam besieged Delhi with his own army. Ibrahim Lodi defeated him there.

Babur named Rana Sanga as one of the five great rulers in India, alongside Krishnadevaraya of the Vijaynagar empire. Sanga was the ruler of Mewar, which had become one of the strongest powers in northern India before he faced Babur.

After the failed attack on Calicut, in which the Portuguese suffered 300 dead and 400 wounded and about 1000 were estimated dead on the Zamorin's side, Afonso de Albuquerque reduced the war against the Zamorin to a blockade in order to pursue bigger goals. As governor of India he conquered Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511. In 1513 he led a campaign to the Red Sea, which required withdrawing the ships blockading Calicut.

The First Luso-Malabarese War drew in famous Portuguese figures such as Vasco da Gama, Pedro Álvares Cabral, Dom Francisco de Almeida and Afonso de Albuquerque. Gama had a ship carrying 10 or 12 of Calicut's wealthiest merchants bombarded and sunk with all on board, and later had envoys of the Zamorin hanged and their bodies floated ashore in a canoe. Duarte Pacheco Pereira's defense of Cochin is considered one of the greatest exploits in the military history of Portugal; cholera broke out in the Zamorin's camp and after seven failed assaults he withdrew.

Mughal rule was also weakened by native resistance. Banda Singh Bahadur led the Sikh Khalsa against the Mughals, and Maharaja Chhatrasal of the Bundela Rajputs fought them and established the Panna State. A later offensive from Lahore, the Vadda Ghalughara, saw 30,000 Sikhs killed.

Rana Sanga was shot by a bullet during the battle and fell unconscious, and Prithviraj Kachwaha and Maldev Rathore of Marwar carried him from the battlefield. After he came round he vowed not to return to Chittor until he had defeated Babur and ousted him, and he wrapped a cloth around his head instead of wearing a turban. While he was preparing another war against Babur, his own nobles, who did not want another conflict with Babur, poisoned him, and he died at Kalpi in January 1528.

literature.text: Under the Mughal Empire in the 16th century, Persian became the official language of the Indian subcontinent. Persian poetry flourished in these regions while post-Safavid Iranian literature stagnated. Only in 1832 did the British army force South Asia to begin conducting business in English.

The first work considered to be Punjabi literature is the 16th century biography of Guru Nanak, called the Janam-sakhi. It was written by his companion Bhai Bala. Some say Punjabi literature may have begun much earlier, perhaps in the 9th or 10th centuries.

Indian style, also known as Sabk-i Hindi, was a literary style in Persian poetry. The name arose because poets and writers affiliated with Indian courts during the Mughal era were particularly notable for using its characteristics in their works.

The first book written by an Indian in English was The Travels of Dean Mahomet, published in 1794. It was a travel narrative by Sake Dean Mahomed. Indian English literature is said to have been evolving since the late 18th century.
After Vaishnavism was introduced in the 18th century, Modern Manipuri came to be written mostly in the Bengali script. This happened under the influence of the Bengali Brahmins.

Between Kalidasa's time and the 18th century, numerous sargabandhas, or long poems divided into cantos, were composed in the classic style. Later ones tended to be more heavily loaded with technical complexity, erudition and extensive decoration.

Lolimbaraja's Harivilasa, composed in the mid 16th century, is named among the later sargabandhas in Sanskrit literature. Such later works tended to be more heavily loaded with technical complexity, erudition and extensive decoration than earlier ones.

science.text: The matchlock mechanism spread eastward during the 16th century, first to Persia after 1514, then to India after 1526 and Afghanistan. It crossed Central Asia to reach Ming Dynasty China around 1513 to 1524, and muskets of this type stayed in use in China and India until the end of the 19th century.

In 1500, Nilakantha Somayaji of the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics revised Aryabhata's elliptical model for the planets Mercury and Venus in his Tantrasamgraha. His equation of the centre for these planets remained the most accurate until the time of Johannes Kepler in the 17th century.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: By the 16th century, South Asians were manufacturing a diverse variety of firearms. Large guns in particular became visible in Tanjore, Dacca, Bijapur and Murshidabad.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Gaṇeśa Daivajna was a sixteenth century astronomer, astrologer and mathematician from western India. He wrote books on methods to predict eclipses and planetary conjunctions, and to make calculations for calendars.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Gaṇeśa Daivajna's most major work was the Grahalaghava, which included ephemeris and calendar calculations. He wrote several other works too, including Siddhantarahasya, Buddhivilāsinī and Laghutithicintamani. He was born around 1507 and was active from 1520 to 1554.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: During the 17th century, Gujarat supplied Europe with saltpeter for use in gunpowder warfare. Bengal and Mālwa also took part in saltpeter production.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The scholar Sadiq Isfahani of Jaunpur compiled an atlas of the parts of the world he held to be suitable for human life. The 32 sheet atlas was part of a larger scholarly work he compiled during 1647.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Guns made of bronze were recovered from Calicut, dated 1504, and from Diu, dated 1533. They show that South Asians were casting large firearms in the early 16th century.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The Dutch, French, Portuguese and English all used Chhapra as a center of saltpeter refining. The town became a hub in the supply of a key ingredient of gunpowder.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The maps in Sadiq Isfahani's 32 sheet atlas were oriented towards the south, as was the case with Islamic works of the era. A reader today would find them upside down compared with modern maps.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

politics.text: The Mughal Empire is conventionally said to have been founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley in Central Asia. In the First Battle of Panipat he defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, and then swept down the plains of northern India. Babur's firearms and cannons let him shatter Ibrahim's armies even though he was at a numerical disadvantage.

The Mughal Empire was created and sustained by military warfare, yet it did not vigorously suppress the cultures and peoples it ruled. Instead it equalised and placated them through new administrative practices and diverse ruling elites.

By 1800 the British East India Company had become the most powerful force in the subcontinent. European trading companies had gradually taken part in Indian political conflicts after Mughal power collapsed following the death of Aurangzeb in 1707.
politics.source_title: Trade between Western Europe and the Mughal Empire in the 17th century

politics.text: Under Krishnadevaraya in the early 16th century, the Vijayanagara Empire subjugated almost all of Southern India's ruling dynasties. It also pushed the Deccan sultanates beyond the Tungabhadra-Krishna River doab and annexed the Gajapati Empire up to the Krishna River.

The Vijayanagara Empire lasted until 1646, but its power declined greatly after a major military defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, when the combined armies of the Deccan sultanates attacked. Two Muslim generals switched sides mid-battle, captured Rama Raya and beheaded him. Sultan Hussain had the severed head stuffed with straw for display. The beheading threw the Vijayanagara army into confusion and it was completely routed, and the sultanates' army then plundered Hampi and reduced it to the ruin it remains today.

During the 17th century the Mughal army became the largest on earth, according to the article's estimates. Its essential form and structure was established by the third emperor, Akbar, and its regular forces were mainly recruited and fielded by Mansabdar officers.

After Bahadur Shah I died in 1712, the Mughal dynasty sank into chaos and violent feuds over control of the throne. In 1719 alone, four emperors successively ascended the throne as figureheads, and Emperor Farrukhsiyar was executed that year. The Sayyid brothers of the Barha family became the de facto sovereigns.
On 23 June 1757, Siraj ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab of Bengal, was betrayed at the Battle of Plassey by Mir Jafar. The British took charge of Bengal and installed Mir Jafar on the throne.

After victory at Buxar in 1764, the East India Company forced Emperor Shah Alam II to appoint it diwan, or revenue collector, of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. By 1773 the company had become the de facto ruler of large areas of the lower Gangetic plain.

In 1765 a Dual Government was established in Bengal, in which the Nawabs ruled on behalf of the British as mere puppets. The system was abolished in 1772 and Bengal came under direct British control. In 1793 the Nawab's Nizamat was also taken away, leaving the Nawabs as pensioners.

Delhi was sacked by the Afghans, and in 1761 the Afghans led by Ahmad Shah Durrani defeated the Maratha Empire in the Third Battle of Panipat. Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, who had made futile attempts to reverse the Mughal decline, ignominiously took temporary refuge with the British to the east. In 1784 the Marathas officially became protectors of the emperor in Delhi.

The Dutch in Malabar were weakened by constant battles with Marthanda Varma of the Travancore royal family and defeated at the Battle of Colachel in 1741. The Treaty of Mavelikkara in 1753 then compelled the Dutch to detach from all political involvements in the region.

philosophy.text: The early modern period saw the flourishing of Navya-Nyāya, meaning 'the new reason'. Raghunatha Siromani, who lived from about 1460 to 1540, founded the tradition. Later thinkers included Jayarama Pancanana and Mahadeva Punatamakara.
Sri Vallabha Acharya, who lived from 1479 to 1531, is described as a very important figure of his era. He founded the Shuddha Advaita, or Pure Non-dualism, school of Vedanta thought.

Satoshi Ogura found no Sanskrit doxography completed up to the end of the sixteenth century that names only Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā, and Vedānta as orthodox systems. He says such a six-part categorisation was not mainstream in Indian philosophy.
Yashovijaya is named among the philosophers who carried Navya-Nyāya, the 'new reason' school, through the early modern period. He formulated a Jain response to it.

The idea of six orthodox systems, or ṣaḍdarśana, has been discussed as a Western or colonial invention. Yet it had probably sprouted in the late medieval or early modern cosmopolitan culture of the subcontinent, before the time of Western impact.

Supriya Gandhi wrote a dissertation on the works of the Mughal prince Dārā Shukūh. She asserts that a later writer named Roy inherited religious discourses from early modern Persian literature, noting that his word-usage resembles that of Dārā.

The 17th-century Indian saint Samarth Ramdas wrote philosophical texts such as Dasbodh, Manache Shlok, and Atmaram. His philosophy was later championed by the spiritual master and social reformer Nana Dharmadhikari, who lived from 1922 to 2008.

Western scholars began debating the relationship between the orthodox āstika and heterodox nāstika philosophies in the 18th and 19th centuries, starting with Indologists and Orientalists. Their work rested on the limited availability of Indian literature and on medieval doxographies.

culture.text: Oil painting and easel painting began in India in the early eighteenth century, when many European artists arrived in search of fame and fortune. Among them were Johann Zoffany, Tilly Kettle, William Hodges, and Thomas Daniell and William Daniell.

In the later half of the 18th century, a distinct genre of watercolour painting on paper and mica developed in India. Called the "company style" or "Patna style", it showed scenes of everyday life, the regalia of princely courts, and native festivities and rituals.

Twelve forts occupied and developed by the Maratha rulers between the 17th and 19th centuries were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025. Eleven are in Maharashtra, which has more than 390 forts, and one, Gingee Fort, is in Tamil Nadu.
European artists were drawn to the courts of India's princely states. The courts patronised the visual and performing arts, and they also needed European-style portraits.
The merchants of the East India Company provided a large market for native art. The company style flourished at first in Murshidabad, and then spread to other cities under British suzerainty.

Authorities consider the company style to be "of hybrid style and undistinguished quality". Even so, its watercolours on paper and mica preserved pictures of everyday life, princely regalia and native festivities of the late 18th century.

The Mughals, Persianized Chagataid Turks, strengthened the Persianate culture of Muslim India after dominating it from 1526. They lured artists and architects from Bukhara, Tabriz, Shiraz and other cities to their courts. Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal.

In the eighteenth century, an earlier generation of British showed an enlightened attitude toward Indian history, monuments, literature, culture and art. By the mid-nineteenth century this had changed, and earlier Indian art was dismissed as "dead" and the stuff of museums.
